title: Childhood trauma is the norm, not the exception, in prison psychiatric care
blurb: Records from 3,400+ adults in Dutch prison psychiatry found over half of men and nearly two-thirds of women had repeated trauma before 18.
summary: This study looked at how common difficult childhood experiences are among people receiving psychiatric care inside Dutch prisons. Researchers reviewed records from more than 3,400 adults and found that over half of the men and nearly two‑thirds of the women had gone through repeated trauma before age 18. Men who had multiple adverse childhood experiences were more likely to have developmental disorders, substance‑use problems, personality disorders, trauma‑related conditions, and a history of violent offenses. For women, repeated childhood trauma was most strongly linked to personality disorders. Overall, the findings highlight how early trauma shapes later mental health and behavior, and they reinforce the need for trauma‑informed care and early intervention—especially in forensic and correctional settings.
journal: Criminal Behaviour and Mental health CBMH

title: How many teens develop PTSD after an earthquake?
blurb: A survey of 234 adolescents found most were resilient — but a meaningful minority showed real distress, with hyperarousal the most common symptom.
summary: This study looked at how many adolescents show signs of PTSD after living through an earthquake. Researchers surveyed 234 teens using a standard PTSD checklist. Most adolescents did not show overall PTSD symptoms, but some did experience specific difficulties—such as re‑experiencing memories, avoiding reminders of the event, changes in mood, and heightened alertness. Hyperarousal symptoms were the most common. Although most teens appeared resilient, a meaningful minority showed signs of distress. The study highlights the importance of early support, resilience‑building programs, and mental‑health resources in schools and communities to help young people cope after natural disasters.
authors: Eka Budiarto, Ira Puspita Agustin, and Nur Intan Kusuma

title: Cluster B personality disorders: what they are and what actually helps
blurb: A review of borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic PD — their origins, the therapies with real evidence, and why culture shapes both.
summary: This review looks at three Cluster B personality disorders—borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic—and explains what they are, why they develop, and which treatments help. These disorders affect how people manage emotions, relate to others, and understand themselves. Research shows they often arise from a mix of genetics, early life stress, and differences in how the brain handles emotions. Therapies like Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Schema Therapy, and Mentalization‑Based Therapy can make a real difference, especially for borderline personality disorder, which carries a high risk of self‑harm. The review also highlights that culture matters. In places like Kenya, stigma and community expectations can make symptoms worse or delay treatment. Because of this, mental‑health care needs to be adapted to fit local cultural realities. Overall, the findings support more flexible diagnostic tools, better‑trained clinicians, and treatment approaches that consider both biology and culture.
journal: Journal of Sociology, Psychology and Religious

title: Kids with ADHD and autism face far higher mental-health risk
blurb: Across 14,000+ young people, those with neurodevelopmental disorders were 3 to 15 times more likely to also have anxiety, depression, or behavioral conditions.
summary: This review looked at how often children and teens with neurodevelopmental disorders—such as ADHD, autism, intellectual disability, and learning disorders—also experience mental‑health conditions like anxiety, depression, or behavioral problems. After examining data from over 14,000 young people, the findings were clear: psychiatric conditions are much more common in children with these disorders than in their neurotypical peers. Rates varied widely, but anxiety and behavioral problems were especially common. Children with neurodevelopmental disorders were between 3 and 15 times more likely to have these additional mental‑health challenges. The study highlights the importance of routinely screening for anxiety, depression, and behavior issues in this group so they can get support early.
journal: The Association of Child and Adolescent Mental Health

title: Who drops out of DBT — and who improves?
blurb: Following 85 people through a DBT program, personality dimensions predicted both improvement and dropout better than symptoms alone.
summary: Borderline Personality Disorder is difficult to treat, and many people drop out of therapy early. This study followed 85 people in a DBT program and found that looking at personality dimensions—not just symptoms—helps explain who improves and who struggles. Most participants showed emotional and interpersonal improvement after 10 weeks, but those with very high negative emotions or psychotic‑like traits improved less, and those with high negative affectivity or anankastia were more likely to drop out. Personality functioning changed the most, suggesting it may be a strong marker of progress. Overall, dimensional personality assessments may help personalize treatment and reduce dropout.
journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and and Clinical Neuroscience

title: The BPD brain is less flexible — and more variable
blurb: fMRI comparing 47 women with BPD to 28 controls found altered brain dynamics tied to childhood trauma and emotion dysregulation.
summary: This study examined how the brains of women with BPD function over time, rather than just how they look at rest. Using resting‑state fMRI, researchers compared 47 women with BPD to 28 healthy controls and analyzed how their brain networks shift, transition, and reorganize. They found that people with BPD show both reduced flexibility in how their brain networks move between states and an unusually wide range of network configurations overall. Greater emotion‑regulation problems were linked to a larger variety of brain states, while fewer transitions between states were tied to more severe BPD symptoms, more childhood trauma, and higher dissociation. Trauma history and emotion‑regulation difficulties also shaped how time spent in certain brain states related to symptom severity. Overall, the findings suggest that altered brain dynamics—less flexibility but more variability—may underlie core BPD features, especially those connected to early trauma and emotion dysregulation.
journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and and Clinical Neuroscience

title: Can machine learning tell bipolar disorder from BPD?
blurb: Five studies, 591 participants: models beat traditional methods, but were far better at spotting bipolar than borderline.
summary: This review examined whether machine learning can help distinguish bipolar disorder from borderline personality disorder—two conditions that are often confused in clinical practice. Out of 60 studies screened, only five met the criteria, covering data from 591 participants. Across these studies, machine‑learning models showed moderate to strong accuracy, performing better than traditional diagnostic methods. However, they were far more accurate at identifying bipolar disorder than borderline personality disorder, highlighting the ongoing difficulty of diagnosing BPD. Models using brain‑imaging features reached about 80% accuracy, and smartphone‑based mood data could differentiate BD, BPD, and healthy controls with about 75% accuracy. Overall, the findings suggest that machine learning holds promise for improving diagnostic precision, but more research is needed before these tools can be reliably used in clinical settings.

title: Do demonstration videos actually teach therapy skills?
blurb: 123 psychology students were randomized to watch a video or reread the text — with a clear winner for learning technique.
summary: This Study tested whether demonstration videos help psychology students learn specific therapeutic techniques. After reading instructional material, 123 students were randomly assigned to either watch a video or reread the text before participating in a simulated therapy session. Students who watched the systemic‑therapy video performed noticeably better in systemic techniques than those who only reviewed the text. However, the psychodynamic video did not lead to better performance compared to rereading. The results suggest that demonstration videos can effectively teach practical skills, but approaches that require deeper theoretical understanding—like psychodynamic therapy—may be harder to learn through video alone. More research is needed to understand how these videos influence long‑term skill development.

title: What a violent hostage incident did to responders' mental health
blurb: Six months on, 192 police special forces and emergency personnel were assessed for quality of life and psychological impact.
summary: This study examined how a highly violent hostage‑taking incident affected the mental health of police special forces compared to other emergency responders. Six months after the event, 192 personnel were assessed for quality of life, anger, and post‑traumatic stress. Special forces officers who were deployed did not differ from their non‑deployed colleagues, suggesting that the operation did not significantly impair their mental health. When compared with firefighters and ambulance personnel who were also on scene, deployed special forces showed better psychological quality of life and lower anger levels, despite facing the most intense operational stress. Regular police officers reported lower environmental quality of life overall. These findings point to greater resilience among special forces and highlight the need to better understand the protective factors that help them withstand traumatic events.
journal: Journal of Police and Criminal Psychology

title: A million genomes reveal what mental illnesses share
blurb: Rather than treating diagnoses as separate boxes, this study mapped the genetic architecture connecting them beneath the surface.
summary: This massive genetic study looked at more than a million people to understand how different mental health disorders are connected beneath the surface. Instead of treating diagnoses like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, PTSD, and anxiety as completely separate, the researchers examined how their genetic patterns overlap. They found that many of these conditions share large portions of the same genetic influences, forming clusters that cut across traditional diagnostic categories. For example, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder share a strong genetic foundation, while depression, PTSD, and anxiety form another closely related group. These shared genetic patterns were linked to specific brain‑related biological pathways. The findings suggest that our current diagnostic system may not fully reflect the underlying biology of mental health conditions—and that future treatments might be more effective if they target these shared genetic and neural pathways rather than focusing on individual diagnoses alone.

title: What drives stigma against tattooed people?
blurb: An Ecuadorian survey used factor analysis to unpack how tattoo stigma operates, especially within the justice system.
summary: Researchers in Ecuador surveyed adults to understand what drives social stigma against tattooed people, particularly within the justice system context. Using a digital questionnaire and statistical factor analysis, they found a clear pattern of negative stereotyping toward tattooed individuals. Interestingly, having tattoos yourself or knowing tattooed people closely was linked to less prejudice, while age, gender, and occupation made no real difference. The takeaway: tattoos still act as a visual cue that triggers snap moral judgments, even in settings like courtrooms where impartiality is supposed to rule, suggesting a real need for training that reduces appearance-based bias in legal and forensic decision-making.
journal: Multidisciplinary Latin American Journal (MLAJ), Vol. 4, No. 2
authors: Héctor Ramiro Carvajal-Romero, Martha Cecilia Carvajal-Blandín, Bernardo Peña-Herrera, Andrés Ricardo Delgado-Reyes

title: What separates forensic from general psychiatric patients with schizophrenia?
blurb: Machine learning compared the two groups to find what actually distinguishes them — beyond the offense itself.
summary: Researchers compared people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders who ended up in forensic psychiatric care (after committing a crime) to those in general psychiatric care, using machine learning to figure out what actually separates the two groups. The surprising part: symptom severity and co-occurring conditions weren't the differentiators at all, both groups looked similar on those measures. What did separate them was social and systemic factors: people in the forensic group were more likely to have experienced childhood social marginalization that persisted into adulthood, and were less likely to have been engaged with the mental health system (fewer prior inpatient/outpatient treatments, weaker treatment adherence) before their current hospitalization. The takeaway challenges a common assumption: it's not that forensic patients have "worse" schizophrenia, it's that gaps in social support and healthcare access are doing most of the work in determining who ends up in the criminal justice system versus standard psychiatric care.
authors: Lena Machetanz, Andreas B. Hofmann, Marc Dörner, Erich Seifritz, Philipp Homan, Johannes Kirchebner

title: Pinpointing where autism and schizophrenia genes switch on
blurb: A preprint mapping risk-gene activity to specific brain regions, not just broad cell types. Not yet peer-reviewed.
summary: Researchers wanted to figure out exactly where in the brain genes linked to autism and schizophrenia are most active, since most prior research could identify the cell types involved (excitatory and inhibitory neurons) but not clearly map which brain regions mattered most. Using a technique called spatial transcriptomics on mouse brain tissue, combined with a new statistical method they developed, the team found that autism-associated genes were most concentrated in the thalamus, with the cortex as a secondary hub. Schizophrenia-linked genes also showed up most strongly in the thalamus, but additionally implicated the hippocampus and cortex. This adds significant weight to a growing idea that the thalamus, traditionally thought of mainly as a sensory relay station, is actually a major player in complex psychiatric conditions, while also showing autism and schizophrenia share some underlying brain circuitry but diverge in others.
journal: bioRxiv (preprint server, not yet peer-reviewed in a journal)
authors: David M. Young, Ruchira Sharma, Narjes Rohani, Chimmi Dema, Lindsay Liang, Bernie Devlin, Devanand S. Manoli, Stephan J. Sanders

title: Is the thalamus different in schizoaffective disorder?
blurb: Detailed imaging broke the thalamus into sub-regions across schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and healthy controls.
summary: Researchers used detailed brain imaging to compare thalamus structure in 25 people with schizophrenia, 20 people with schizoaffective disorder, and 26 healthy controls, breaking the thalamus down into its individual sub-regions (nuclei) rather than treating it as one uniform structure. They found that people with schizoaffective disorder had a notably smaller right-side thalamus overall, plus specific reductions in nuclei tied to sensory processing, emotional regulation, and pain. People with straightforward schizophrenia didn't show this same pattern to the same degree. This suggests schizoaffective disorder, which blends psychotic and mood symptoms, may have its own distinct brain signature rather than just being a hybrid or milder variant of schizophrenia, and could eventually help refine how these conditions are diagnosed and distinguished from each other.
authors: Eren Tanrıseven, Ergin Sağtaş, Osman Zulkif Topak, Muhammet Gündüz, Ceren Arıbakır Dogruyol

title: Two low-cost interventions for grandiose delusions
blurb: Indonesian nurse-researchers tested simple non-pharmacological approaches in a single case of schizophrenia with grandiose delusions.
summary: Nurses and researchers from Universitas Padjadjaran in Indonesia tested two simple, low-cost non-pharmacological interventions on a 21-year-old man with schizophrenia who was experiencing grandiose delusions, meaning he held strong false beliefs about having exceptional power, status, or identity. Over four sessions across one week, each lasting 15 to 30 minutes, the patient played card matching games and wrote in a journal for self-reflection. The card game was designed to improve concentration and the ability to follow rules, two skills that are often disrupted when delusions dominate thinking. The journaling component asked the patient to write down his thoughts and gradually work toward recognizing which beliefs were disconnected from reality. By the end of the week, the patient showed reduced intensity in his grandiose beliefs, better concentration, more controlled behavior, and speech that more closely matched reality. The researchers are clear that this didn't result in full recovery, and the interventions worked best alongside the patient's existing medication. The broader point the paper makes is that structured activities grounding someone in rules, sequencing, and concrete self-reflection may help counteract the reality distortion of delusions as part of a combined care approach.
journal: Journal of Nursing, Vol. 1, No. 2 (2026), pp. 81–88
authors: Sausandha Yasma Chaimira, Indra Maulana, Efri Widianti (all from Universitas Padjadjaran, Indonesia)

title: A new 14-item scale for antisocial personality disorder
blurb: The SEPBA-APD aims to bridge categorical and dimensional approaches to diagnosing ASPD.
summary: Researchers developed and tested a new 14-item questionnaire called the SEPBA-APD for measuring antisocial personality disorder, designed to bridge two different ways psychologists currently diagnose personality disorders: the traditional checklist-style DSM-5 criteria and newer dimensional models (AMPD and HiTOP) that treat traits as existing on a spectrum rather than simply present or absent. They tested it on 600 people from the general community and 149 incarcerated individuals. The scale held up well statistically, showing strong internal consistency and good ability to distinguish people with antisocial traits from those without (with accuracy scores in the 85 to 89% range, which is considered strong for psychological diagnostic accuracy). The bigger picture: this gives clinicians and researchers a brief, validated tool that doesn't force them to choose between "do you have ASPD or not" and "how much ASPD-like traits do you have," letting them capture both at once.
authors: L. Torres-Rosado, O. M. Lozano, M. Sánchez-García, L. Maciel, and Miguel Basto-Pereira

title: Virtual reality art therapy for borderline personality disorder
blurb: Eight participants completed four weekly VR-based art sessions, with wellbeing measured throughout. A small pilot, not proof.
summary: Researchers tested whether combining art therapy with virtual reality could help people with borderline personality disorder. Eight participants completed four weekly VR-based art sessions, and the team measured changes in wellbeing, emotion regulation, depression, anxiety, and stress using standard validated questionnaires. The results were encouraging: participants showed improvements across wellbeing and emotion regulation, plus reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress, with anxiety showing a statistically significant drop. People also reported finding the sessions genuinely helpful. That said, this is a small pilot study with only eight participants and no control group, so it's an early, promising signal rather than confirmed evidence, and the authors themselves note larger studies are needed before drawing firm conclusions.
journal: Journal of Creativity in Mental Health, Vol. 21, Issue 2 (2026)
authors: Beatriz Silva, Sara de Sousa, João Viana, Joana Gomes, Raquel Simões de Almeida

title: Can a single dose of psilocybin help people quit cocaine?
blurb: A randomized controlled trial tested psilocybin plus structured psychotherapy for a disorder with no approved medications.
summary: Researchers ran a rigorous randomized controlled trial testing whether a single dose of psilocybin, combined with structured psychotherapy, could help people quit cocaine, a disorder with no currently approved medications. Forty adults with cocaine use disorder, most of them Black and lower-income, a population historically underrepresented in psychedelic research, were randomly assigned to receive either psilocybin or an active placebo, alongside the same therapy protocol either way. Neither participants, therapists, nor the people analyzing the data knew who got what. The results were striking: people who got psilocybin had far more cocaine-free days, were about 18 times more likely to achieve complete abstinence through 180 days, and had a much lower risk of relapsing compared to the placebo group. No serious side effects occurred, though the drug's effects made it hard to fully disguise who'd received it, a known challenge in psychedelic research. While the sample size is small and a few questions remain (like exactly how much unblinding affected the results), this is the first trial of its kind for cocaine use disorder and represents a genuinely promising signal for a notoriously hard-to-treat addiction.
authors: Peter S. Hendricks, Sara N. Lappan, Richard C. Shelton, Adrienne C. Lahti, Karen L. Cropsey, Matthew W. Johnson, Melissa Bradley, Otto Simonsson, Lori L. Davis, Daniel H. Grossman, Cynthia E. Ortiz

title: What GLP-1 drugs do to depression and anxiety
blurb: Swedish records for ~100,000 people compared periods when the same individuals were and weren't taking GLP-1 medications.
summary: Researchers used Swedish national health records to study nearly 100,000 people who already had depression or anxiety and were taking antidiabetic medication, comparing periods when the same individuals were and weren't using GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide and liraglutide. This "within-individual" design is a clever way to reduce bias, since it compares a person against themselves rather than against a different group of people. The findings ran counter to some earlier, more alarming reports: GLP-1 use was linked to a lower risk of worsening mental illness, including reduced psychiatric hospitalizations, fewer mental-health-related sick leaves, and more than a 40% lower risk of self-harm. Semaglutide specifically showed a 42% reduction in worsening mental illness compared to periods of non-use. This adds an important, large-scale data point to a previously mixed picture, some past studies had suggested these drugs might worsen mood, while this one suggests the opposite, though as an observational cohort study (not a randomized trial), it can show a strong association but can't fully prove the drugs are causing the improvement.
journal: The Lancet Psychiatry, Vol. 13, Issue 4, pages 327-335
authors: Heidi Taipale, Mark Taylor, Ellenor Mittendorfer-Rutz, Antti Tanskanen, Jari Tiihonen

title: How early-life stress rewires the gut
blurb: A mouse model of maternal separation traced the actual mechanism linking early stress to long-term digestive problems.
summary: Researchers wanted to understand exactly how early-life stress leads to long-term digestive problems, since the gut-brain connection was known but the underlying mechanism wasn't clear. Using a mouse model of early maternal separation, they found that early stress caused heightened gut pain sensitivity, sex-specific problems with intestinal movement, and lasting structural changes to the gut's own nervous system, including more serotonin-related nerve activity. They traced this to two separate culprits: sex hormones appeared to drive the pain sensitivity (blocking gonadal hormones reversed it), while overactive sympathetic nervous system signaling drove the motility problems (blocking that signaling restored normal gut movement). Serotonin pathways seemed to influence both issues. To confirm this matters in humans, not just mice, they analyzed two large pediatric population groups and found that mothers' mental health struggles were consistently linked to higher rates of gut-brain disorders in their children, mirroring the lab findings. The bigger picture: childhood stress doesn't just affect mental health, it can physically rewire two separate nerve pathways in the gut, and because pain and motility are driven by different mechanisms, future treatments may need to target them separately rather than with one blanket approach.
authors: Najjar S, Kildegaard H, Talati A, and colleagues

title: Brain chemistry differences across anxiety disorders
blurb: 25 brain-imaging studies pooled to compare choline and other chemical levels across social, generalized, and panic anxiety.
summary: Researchers pooled data from 25 brain-imaging studies (using a technique called proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which measures brain chemical levels non-invasively) covering social anxiety disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and panic disorder, comparing 370 people with these conditions to 342 healthy controls. The standout finding: choline-containing compounds, molecules involved in maintaining cell membranes and supporting brain signaling, were consistently lower across cortical brain regions in people with any of the three anxiety disorders, especially in the prefrontal cortex, with about an 8% average reduction. Notably, this pattern held steady across all three diagnoses, suggesting it's a shared feature of anxiety in general rather than specific to one disorder. The researchers propose that chronic anxiety keeps the brain's arousal system on overdrive, and stress-related brain chemicals like norepinephrine may increase the brain's demand for choline faster than it can be replenished, gradually depleting it. They also found a related dip in a marker of neuronal health. While this doesn't prove cause and effect, the authors suggest it raises an interesting future question: could choline supplementation eventually have a role in treating anxiety, an idea worth further dedicated research before anyone draws conclusions.

title: Why some people hear voices: testing the inner-speech theory
blurb: A long-standing but hard-to-prove idea about how the brain fails to recognize its own inner speech, finally put to the test.
summary: This study tested a long-standing but hard-to-prove theory about why people with schizophrenia sometimes hear voices that aren't there. The idea is that the brain normally dampens its response to your own inner speech (the silent voice in your head), and a malfunction in that dampening might cause inner thoughts to be misperceived as external voices. The researchers had three groups, people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders who currently hear voices, people with the same diagnosis who don't, and healthy controls, silently imagine a syllable at a precise moment while simultaneously hearing an actual spoken syllable that either matched or didn't match what they were imagining, all while measuring brain activity via EEG. Healthy controls showed the expected pattern: their brains dampened the response to the real sound when their inner speech matched it, as if recognizing "I already produced this." People who currently experienced hallucinations showed the opposite effect entirely, their brains actually amplified the response when inner and outer speech matched, instead of suppressing it. People with the same diagnosis but no current hallucinations showed yet another distinct pattern. The more severe a person's hallucinations were, the more pronounced this reversed brain signal became. This gives real, measurable, brain-based evidence for the idea that auditory hallucinations may stem from a specific breakdown in how the brain distinguishes self-generated thoughts from the outside world, rather than being a vague or unexplainable symptom.
authors: Thomas J. Whitford, Lawrence Kin-hei Chung, Oren Griffiths, Bradley N. Jack, Mike E. Le Pelley, Kevin M. Spencer, Ana R. Barreiros, Anthony W. Harrison, Nathan T. Han, Sol Libesman, Daniel Pearson, Ruth B. Elijah, Marianthe Godwin, Carla Haroutonian, Angela Nickerson, Sandra Sau-man Chan, George Heung-chuen Chong, Gary Kar-wai Lau, Yip-chau Wong, Jason Wai-yiu Wong, Judith M. Ford, Daniel H. Mathalon, Anthony W. F. Harris, Suzanne Ho-wai So

title: Schizophrenia genetics beyond European ancestry
blurb: Most schizophrenia genetics has studied European populations. This study set out to close a major gap in the science.
summary: Most genetic research on schizophrenia has historically focused on people of European ancestry, leaving a major gap in scientific understanding for the rest of the world. This study, led by researchers at Mount Sinai, SUNY Downstate, and the VA, conducted the largest genome-wide association study of schizophrenia ever done in people of African ancestry. The team identified more than 100 new genetic regions linked to schizophrenia that hadn't been clearly detected before, many of which are more common specifically in people of African ancestry, explaining why earlier, less diverse studies missed them entirely. Crucially, even though the specific genetic variants differ across populations (different genetic "spelling changes," as the researchers put it), those variants tend to disrupt the same underlying genes, brain cell types, and signaling pathways tied to maintaining balanced brain activity. In other words, schizophrenia's biological roots appear to be fundamentally shared across populations worldwide, even when the genetic risk factors that trigger it vary. The researchers are careful to note that none of this allows for predicting who will or won't develop schizophrenia, since environmental, social, and cultural factors matter just as much and aren't captured by genetics alone. The bigger picture: broader representation in genetic research doesn't just help one population, it strengthens confidence in the universal biology of the disorder and lays groundwork for future treatments that could work across diverse populations.

title: Finding the brain basis of BPD identity disturbance
blurb: Researchers studied identity disturbance as early as possible — before medication or comorbidity could muddy the picture.
summary: Researchers wanted to find a measurable brain basis for one of BPD's defining features: a disturbed sense of identity, by studying it as early as possible, before medication or other psychiatric conditions could complicate the picture. They scanned 27 medication-naïve adolescent girls with BPD and no other psychiatric diagnoses, alongside 28 matched healthy peers, using fMRI while participants answered true-or-false questions about themselves, about an acquaintance, or about neutral facts. When comparing self-reflection to simple fact-processing, the BPD group showed markedly reduced activity in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region tied to top-down cognitive control, along with weaker activity in some visual and parietal regions. This pattern was specific to thinking about themselves; when reflecting on another person, the difference showed up in a completely different brain region, the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex, and turned out to reflect something different: a failure to properly "quiet down" that region during the unrelated fact-processing task, rather than a problem with other-reflection itself. In healthy adolescents, self- and other-reflection typically activate very similar brain networks. The fact that BPD patients showed two distinct breakdowns in two different regions suggests these two processes might become oddly decoupled from each other in the disorder. The researchers interpret the main finding, the prefrontal cortex dip during self-reflection, as a sign of weakened top-down regulation when processing identity-related information, giving an early, measurable neurobiological clue to where BPD's hallmark identity disturbance might originate.
authors: Pilar Salgado-Pineda, Marc Ferrer, Natàlia Calvo, Juan D. Duque-Yemail, Xavier Costa, Àlex Rué, Violeta Pérez-Rodriguez, Josep Antoni Ramos-Quiroga, Cristina Veciana-Verdaguer, Paola Fuentes-Claramonte, Raymond Salvador, Peter J. McKenna, Edith Pomarol-Clotet

title: Crying in therapy predicts better outcomes
blurb: Across 58 patients, those who cried more intensely and longer in early sessions reported better results later.
summary: New research shows crying in therapy isn't just emotional release—it may actually predict better outcomes. A study of 58 patients found that when people cried with greater intensity and for longer during early sessions, they reported stronger connections with their therapists and deeper, more meaningful sessions. Therapists noticed it too. Even more striking: patients who cried more intensely and longer showed greater improvement in anxiety and overall mental health symptoms by the end of treatment. What prompts these moments? Mostly therapist interventions encouraging patients to express and explore their feelings—plus interpretations that offered new ways of understanding their experiences. The takeaway: the quality of crying (how deeply and how long) matters more than just whether it happens. Emotional depth in therapy seems to be doing real work.

title: Cognitive training in mandated treatment
blurb: A 10-session group program combining cognitive and goal-management training, tested with 35 participants before and after.
summary: This study tested a 10‑session group program that combined cognitive training and goal‑management training for people in mandated treatment. Thirty‑five participants completed cognitive tests before and after the program. Results showed clear improvements in executive functions—better inhibition, planning, and cognitive flexibility. However, these gains didn’t translate into changes in self‑reported behavior or reductions in substance use. Overall, the intervention strengthened cognitive skills but didn’t meaningfully affect substance‑use outcomes in the short term.

title: Does the PTSD checklist catch symptom exaggeration across cultures?
blurb: 115 contractors were evaluated to test whether a common PTSD measure works outside Western populations.
summary: This study looked at whether a common PTSD questionnaire can reliably spot when someone is exaggerating or faking symptoms—not just in Western countries, but in African populations too. Researchers evaluated 115 contractors from Uganda, Kenya, and Zimbabwe who had worked on U.S. military bases and were being assessed for PTSD in a legal/compensation setting. They compared people who gave credible answers with those who didn’t. While the two groups looked the same in terms of background, the PTSD checklist did a good job telling them apart. The cutoffs that worked best were almost identical to those used in North America. Overall, the results show that this PTSD tool works well across cultures and can be trusted in international forensic evaluations.

title: Changing the wording changes your depression score
blurb: A randomized trial altered only the instructions on the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 — and the same people scored differently.
summary: We treat depression and anxiety questionnaires like neutral rulers, but this randomized trial shows the ruler can bend. Researchers recruited 200 U.S. adults who had been diagnosed with or treated for major depression or generalized anxiety, and had each person complete the two most widely used screeners, the PHQ-9 (depression) and GAD-7 (anxiety), twice in one sitting. The control group got standard instructions both times. The intervention group got standard instructions first, but before the second round they were simply reminded to pay attention to the wording of the instructions, with emphasis on the word “bothered” (as in, how often have you been bothered by these problems). That tiny nudge produced a real drop: intervention participants scored about 2.6 points lower on both the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, and were roughly 14 times more likely to show a greater-than-20% reduction in their depression score. The point isn’t that anyone was faking, it’s that these tools aren’t perfectly objective, and small differences in how they’re administered can move scores enough to matter in clinics, research, and mental-health apps. A strong case for standardizing exactly how screeners are delivered.

title: The self-esteem myth
blurb: A longitudinal meta-analysis of 27 studies found no robust evidence that low self-esteem causes later behavior problems.
summary: “Boost a kid’s self-esteem and their behavior problems will fade” is one of the most durable ideas in pop psychology. This longitudinal meta-analysis put it to the test, and didn’t find the causal link. Researchers pooled 27 studies (25 independent samples) following 38,489 young people, average age 12, over time. At first glance, low self-esteem and “externalizing” problems (aggression, rule-breaking, acting out) did travel together, showing a weak negative correlation. But correlation isn’t cause. When the researchers used cross-lagged models, the approach that asks whether earlier self-esteem actually predicts later behavior problems after accounting for starting levels, the effect vanished in both directions. Earlier self-esteem did not predict later externalizing problems, and earlier behavior problems did not predict later self-esteem. These null results held steady across age, sex, and study methods. The practical point for educators and parents: don’t expect self-esteem programs to fix behavior problems, and don’t assume that curbing misbehavior will automatically build self-worth. They’re related, but neither reliably drives the other, a useful myth to retire.

title: Does vitamin D help depression?
blurb: 108 young people with both major depression and low vitamin D were given supplements. The effect was real but modest.
summary: Vitamin D gets talked about as a natural mood fix, so this trial is a useful, careful reality check. Researchers in Taiwan studied 108 young people (ages 10–24) who had both major depression and low vitamin D, giving them either 4,800 IU of vitamin D3 daily for 8 weeks or a placebo. The headline result is nuanced: overall, vitamin D did NOT beat placebo for depression itself. It did modestly reduce anxiety in the randomized vitamin D group. And when researchers zoomed in on participants with moderate-to-severe depression, that subgroup showed reductions in both depression and anxiety versus placebo, though the adolescent slice of that subgroup didn’t clearly benefit. No safety problems (like high calcium) appeared. So what does it mean? For a young person who is genuinely vitamin-D deficient and more severely depressed, supplementation might help as one piece of care. But this is a small, exploratory study, and it does not show that vitamin D lifts depression for everyone. It’s a promising lead worth bigger trials, not a standalone treatment, and definitely not a reason to skip established care. Helpful for some, not a cure.

title: Treating moral injury in veterans
blurb: A pilot trial compared two therapies designed for the lasting pain of violating one's own deepest values.
summary: Moral injury, the lasting pain of having done, witnessed, or failed to prevent something that violates your deepest values, is common in veterans and notoriously hard to treat. This pilot trial developed and tested two therapies designed specifically for it. Seventy-four war-zone-deployed veterans were randomly assigned to either Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Moral Injury (ACT-MI), which focuses on making room for painful thoughts while re-engaging with valued living, or Present-Centered Therapy for Moral Injury (PCT-MI), a structured comparison approach focused on current problems. Both are 15-session programs combining group and individual work. As a pilot, the goal was feasibility and acceptability rather than proving which one wins, and on that front both did well: veterans rated both therapies highly, and described ACT-MI in particular as improving daily functioning and offering alternatives to suicidal behavior and substance use. A measure of psychosocial functioning suggested larger improvement in the ACT-MI group, but the study wasn’t designed or powered to confirm that. The real significance is that both approaches proved workable and welcomed, clearing the way for a full-scale efficacy trial. For a wound medicine has struggled to reach, having credible, testable options is a meaningful step.

title: An app for depression after breast cancer
blurb: 313 women were enrolled in a trial of a fully automated, publicly available program — because there aren't enough therapists.
summary: Depression and anxiety are common after breast cancer, but there aren’t nearly enough therapists to go around, which is why this trial tested a fully automated, publicly available app-based program. Researchers enrolled 313 women within five years of a breast cancer diagnosis who had elevated depression or anxiety, and randomly assigned them (2:1) to either an 8-week digital mental health program (a suite of five clinically focused apps called IntelliCare) or a patient-education app that served as an active comparison. Both groups improved meaningfully over time, but the digital program had an edge specifically for anxiety, producing significantly greater reductions than the education app. For depression, the digital program’s advantage did not reach statistical significance. The trial also tested whether adding a human coach helped people who barely used the app in week one; coaching did boost how many days they engaged. The bottom line: a scalable, self-guided app can help breast cancer survivors, particularly with anxiety, and a light touch of human support can keep less-engaged users coming back. It won’t replace therapy for everyone, but it can extend real help to survivors who otherwise couldn’t access care.

title: Can a short video reduce suicide-loss stigma?
blurb: A large randomized trial tested whether brief video content could shift the judgment suicide-loss survivors face.
summary: People who lose someone to suicide carry a heavy grief, and often a second burden: public stigma, the subtle judgment that they were somehow disconnected, weak, or to blame. This large randomized trial asked whether something as simple as a short video could soften that stigma. Researchers recruited 1,351 adults aged 18–50 and randomly showed them either a brief first-person video of a suicide-loss survivor sharing their story, or a psychoeducational control video. Compared with the control, people who watched the survivor’s narrative showed clear reductions in stigma right afterward and still partially at 30 days. The biggest shifts were in specific judgments: seeing survivors as “disconnected” fell by about 24% and “cowardly” by 16%, with smaller but real drops in viewing them as “immoral” or “irresponsible.” The effect faded somewhat over the month, suggesting these messages need repeating to stick. Still, the promise is significant: a low-cost, easily shared video, the kind of thing that fits naturally on social media, can measurably move a community from blame toward empathy. For survivors, that shift in the social climate around them isn’t just kind; it can support their recovery.

title: Group therapy measurably lowered cortisol
blurb: 60 adults randomized to an 8-week integrative group program — with the body's stress chemistry as the outcome.
summary: Can talk-based therapy leave a measurable fingerprint on your body’s stress chemistry? This randomized trial went looking for one with unusual rigor. Sixty adults were randomly assigned to either an 8-week integrative group program, combining social-emotional skills, slow breathing with heart-rate-variability biofeedback, and cognitive reappraisal, or a dose-matched active control. Rather than relying on a single measurement, researchers profiled the stress hormone cortisol across multiple days from saliva, and also measured cortisol built up in hair, which reflects roughly the prior month. The intervention group showed a clear drop in daily cortisol output compared with control, and that reduction was still present at the 6-month follow-up. Hair cortisol was lower too, backing up the saliva findings, and related stress markers decreased as well. One honest caveat: the trial ran at a single site and was partly commercially funded, so independent replication matters. But the design, multi-day profiling plus hair analysis against an active comparison, makes this a stronger-than-usual signal that structured psychological skills training can register in the body’s stress system, not just in how people say they feel.

title: 25 years of US adolescent mental-health deaths
blurb: CDC records for ages 15–24 from 1999 to 2023, tracking how mental illness figured into young Americans' deaths.
summary: How has mental illness figured into young Americans’ deaths over the past quarter century? This study took the long view, analyzing CDC records of deaths among U.S. adolescents and young adults aged 15–24 from 1999 to 2023 where a mental or behavioral disorder was listed as a contributing cause. Over those 25 years, 67,984 such deaths were recorded, about 6.4 per 100,000 young people. The trend wasn’t a simple straight line up: researchers identified two distinct periods of increase (1999–2006 and 2009–2021), while the overall long-run trend was relatively stable. What stands out most are the disparities. Young men and those aged 20–24 died at higher rates than young women and 15–19-year-olds. American Indian and Alaska Native youth carried the heaviest burden of any racial or ethnic group, and deaths clustered geographically, with the highest rates in the South. The authors frame this less as a single alarm and more as a map of where help is failing to reach: persistent and emerging gaps that call for targeted, equity-focused prevention and better access to mental health and substance-use care for the young people and communities most affected.

title: Does seeing clients more often help them finish PTSD treatment?
blurb: A meta-regression across 84 study arms asked whether session frequency drives treatment completion.
summary: A practical question for anyone delivering trauma therapy: does seeing clients more often help them actually finish treatment? This meta-regression pulled together data from a large PTSD clinical-trials repository, 84 study arms across 66 studies, to look at how session frequency and therapy type relate to completion. It focused on three gold-standard treatments: cognitive processing therapy (CPT), prolonged exposure (PE), and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR). A few patterns emerged. Compared with CPT, patients were somewhat less likely to complete PE overall, but when PE was delivered more frequently than weekly, the odds of completing it doubled. Patients were also more than twice as likely to complete EMDR than CPT, though for EMDR the frequency effect wasn’t statistically clear. The researchers also flagged a messy problem in the field: only about a third of trials even defined what “completing treatment” means, making comparisons harder than they should be. The clinical upshot is that scheduling isn’t just logistics, for exposure-based therapy in particular, tighter session spacing may help more people cross the finish line. And the research world could help itself by agreeing on what completion actually means.

title: Mentalization therapy for antisocial personality disorder
blurb: A UK randomized trial offers cautious hope for a condition widely assumed to be untreatable.
summary: Antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) is one of the conditions clinicians feel most helpless about, strongly linked to offending and widely assumed to be untreatable. This UK randomized controlled trial offers cautious hope, and unusually, it looked at the money too. Men with ASPD who had been convicted of an offence and were on community probation in England and Wales were randomized to receive either mentalization-based treatment adapted for ASPD (a therapy that builds the capacity to understand one’s own and others’ mental states) added to usual probation, or probation as usual alone. Researchers tracked outcomes over 24 months from a whole-society perspective, health care, criminal justice, and the broader costs of offending. Missing data made firm conclusions difficult, but the available picture favored the therapy: participants who got it tended to spend less time in custody, showed lower aggression, and the approach came out cost-effective, with each unit reduction in aggression associated with roughly £93 in savings. Quality-of-life differences were minimal. As a first full economic evaluation in this population it’s preliminary, but it suggests a wall clinicians rarely get through may not be as solid as assumed, and that treating ASPD could pay for itself through less aggression and less custody.

title: Treating trauma and addiction at the same time in young people
blurb: Clinicians have long debated treating them one at a time. This trial treated both at once, in ages 12–25.
summary: When trauma and substance use occur together, clinicians have long debated whether to treat them one at a time or both at once, and caution often wins, especially with young people, out of fear that facing trauma memories might worsen substance use. This trial challenges that caution. Researchers in Sydney randomized 55 young people aged 12–25 with co-occurring PTSD and substance use to either COPE-A, an integrated, exposure-based therapy that tackles trauma and substance use simultaneously (adapted from an adult program), or person-centred supportive counselling. The integrated approach worked, and worked faster. By four months, PTSD symptom severity had dropped significantly more in the COPE-A group, and only 20% still met criteria for PTSD, compared with about 67% in the counselling group. Both groups reduced their substance use over time, with no clear difference there, and importantly there were no treatment-related adverse events, directly countering the worry that exposure work is too risky for this age group. Young people were also more satisfied with COPE-A. It’s a modest-sized study, but as the first of its kind in adolescents and young adults to show integrated treatment beating a control on PTSD outcomes, it makes a strong case for treating the whole picture at once rather than waiting.

title: The real link between childhood maltreatment and narcissism
blurb: Across 2,157 people, early harm didn't simply 'create narcissists' — it shaped which narcissistic traits emerged.
summary: “Narcissists are made by their childhoods” is a popular claim, but this study shows the real link is more specific and more interesting than the meme. Researchers drew on five cohorts totaling 2,157 people, including healthy volunteers and a large clinical sample (mostly people with major depression, plus schizophrenia-spectrum, bipolar, and stress-related conditions). They measured childhood maltreatment alongside two distinct faces of narcissism: “admiration” (the grandiose, self-promoting, look-how-great-I-am side) and “rivalry” (the defensive, antagonistic, protect-my-status-by-putting-others-down side). Childhood maltreatment was linked to lower admiration and higher rivalry, small effects, but consistent. In plain terms, early harm wasn’t associated with more confident grandiosity; if anything it tracked with less of it, and with more of the brittle, defensive kind of narcissism. Emotional abuse, emotional neglect, and physical neglect were the maltreatment types most consistently tied to this pattern. The associations differed somewhat between healthy and clinical groups, and because the data are cross-sectional, this shows correlation, not proof of cause. Still, it reframes a common story: adversity doesn’t simply create narcissists. It may shape which narcissistic traits emerge, nudging people toward the guarded, rivalrous style rather than the openly grandiose one.

title: Lifestyle medicine for depression, without a therapist
blurb: A three-arm trial of an 8-week program delivered by app, by booklet, or not at all.
summary: Can “lifestyle medicine,” the unglamorous basics of activity, diet, sleep, and stress management, actually treat depression when delivered without a therapist? This three-arm trial says yes, at least in the short term. Researchers in Hong Kong randomized 122 adults with probable depression to one of three groups: the same 8-week multicomponent lifestyle program delivered through a smartphone app, the identical program delivered as printed booklets, or a waitlist. The core content was the same across both active arms, psychoeducation, physical activity, nutrition, sleep and stress management, goal-setting, and motivation, just packaged differently. Both worked. At the end of the program, 78% of the app group and 55% of the booklet group had achieved clinically meaningful improvement in depression, versus just under 20% of those left waiting, and the gains held at one- and three-month follow-ups. The app had extra advantages for stress and healthy habits, while the booklet uniquely helped insomnia. The honest caveats: it’s a modest sample, and it was compared with a waitlist rather than against established treatments like therapy or medication. But as a low-cost, scalable option, especially the app, which needs no clinician time, it’s a genuinely encouraging result for reaching people who can’t easily access traditional care.

title: The first non-dopamine schizophrenia drug in 70 years
blurb: Nearly every antipsychotic since the 1950s has blocked dopamine. A muscarinic drug works a completely different way.
summary: For over 70 years, almost every antipsychotic has worked the same fundamental way, by blocking the brain’s dopamine D2 receptors. That approach helps many people, but it often does little for the “negative” symptoms (like flattened emotion and social withdrawal) and cognitive problems that most shape day-to-day life, and it can bring heavy side effects. This review charts a genuine turning point. In 2024, the FDA approved KarXT, a first-in-class drug that skips dopamine entirely and instead activates muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (specifically the M1 and M4 subtypes), the first non-D2 antipsychotic mechanism in more than seven decades. Late-stage (Phase III) trials show it improves both positive and negative symptom domains, with a favorable metabolic profile: no clinically meaningful weight gain or blood-sugar disruption, unlike many older drugs. Early hints suggest possible cognitive benefits for those who start with impairment, though that needs confirmation, and long-term safety data are still limited. The review also covers a second experimental route, glutamate-targeting drugs like GlyT1 inhibitors, but there the trial results have been inconsistent, leaving that path uncertain. The big picture: muscarinic drugs are the first proven alternative to the dopamine playbook, opening a real new direction for a disorder where progress has been painfully slow.

title: Does EMDR really work?
blurb: A meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials: EMDR clearly beats no treatment, but roughly ties other active therapies.
summary: EMDR, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, is one of the most popular and most debated trauma therapies, built on the unusual idea that guided eye movements while recalling a trauma can help the brain reprocess it. Does it hold up? This systematic review and meta-analysis gathered randomized controlled trials of EMDR for PTSD published over two decades and pooled 11 of them. The answer is a qualified yes. EMDR produced a significant reduction in PTSD symptom severity overall, but the size of the benefit depended heavily on what it was compared against. Against “passive” controls (like waitlists or no treatment), EMDR looked strongly effective. Against other “active” treatments, established trauma therapies, the advantage shrank and the two came out roughly comparable. The authors also note that most included trials had some methodological weaknesses, so confidence isn’t absolute. The practical reading: EMDR genuinely works for PTSD and clearly beats doing nothing, but the evidence doesn’t crown it superior to other proven trauma treatments, it’s one effective option among several, not a magic bullet. As always, the comparison you choose shapes the story you tell.
authors: Ryan Gabriel A. Peji, et al.

title: There are two kinds of narcissism
blurb: Not every narcissist brags about being the best. Some brag about being the kindest.
summary: When we picture a narcissist, we usually imagine the braggart chasing status and admiration. But researchers increasingly recognize a second flavor: the “communal” narcissist, who inflates themselves not through competence but through goodness, “I’m the most caring, the most moral, the most selfless person in the room.” This study examined how these styles connect to self-enhancement in 306 Polish and Italian university students. Participants completed measures of four narcissism dimensions (admiration, rivalry, sanctity, and heroism) plus two ways people puff themselves up: “overclaiming” (confidently claiming to know things that don’t actually exist) and the “better-than-average” effect. The pattern was telling. Among the agentic, status-oriented traits, only admiration reliably drove self-enhancement. Among the communal traits, both sanctity and heroism did, communal narcissists really do self-enhance, just in the moral domain. There were cultural wrinkles too: in Italy, communal self-enhancement showed up mainly in the milder better-than-average effect. The sample is small and made up of students, so it’s a piece of a larger puzzle rather than the last word. But the message is worth sitting with: the loudest “look how good a person I am” can be its own form of self-obsession, and narcissism doesn’t always announce itself as arrogance, sometimes it wears the mask of virtue.

title: Do psychedelics harm memory?
blurb: An exploratory study of working memory after a single dose. Reassuring — but it had no control group.
summary: As psychedelics move toward mainstream mental-health treatment, an important question often gets less attention than the hype: do they harm cognition? This exploratory study looked specifically at working memory, the mental scratchpad you use to hold and manipulate information. Healthy volunteers received a single dose of either psilocybin or MDMA (29 people analyzed per drug, with 16 taking both after a washout period), and completed a demanding memory task while researchers recorded brain activity with EEG, before dosing, days after, and again at a three-month follow-up. The reassuring result: no evidence of working-memory impairment from a single dose of either drug. If anything, brain recordings showed lasting changes in memory-related neural activity, and memory task accuracy actually improved by three months. The crucial caveat, which the authors themselves stress, is that this study had no control group, so improvements could partly reflect practice on the task or other factors, not the drugs alone. That’s why this counts as a reassuring signal rather than proof. Still, for a field where fears of cognitive damage are frequently raised, finding no sign of memory harm from controlled single doses is a meaningful, if preliminary, data point, and a good example of why careful measurement should temper both the fear and the hype.

title: Younger substance users show more psychosis and violence
blurb: 264 patients followed for six months in Spain, comparing those whose use began early to longer-term older users.
summary: Does the age at which someone’s substance use takes hold change how the illness looks? This six-month study from Spain suggests it does, in ways that matter for treatment. Researchers followed 264 patients with substance use disorder at an addiction treatment unit, splitting them into two groups: those with “prolonged” use histories (aged 55 or older, or 25-plus years of use) and those with shorter trajectories (younger and fewer years of use). Everyone completed structured interviews and validated measures of quality of life, impulsivity, autistic traits, addiction severity, psychotic symptoms, and violence. The younger group stood out for a heavier psychiatric burden: significantly more auditory and visual hallucinations and persecutory (paranoid) delusions at the start, along with more violence-related behavior. Over the six months, both groups reduced physical aggression in some contexts, though verbal aggression (insults and threats) rose. Notably, screening positive for ADHD, autistic traits, or high impulsivity didn’t predict who stayed in treatment; instead, poorer physical functioning predicted dropping out among longer-term users. The takeaway is a case for age-sensitive addiction care: younger people arriving with substance problems may carry a sharper load of psychosis and violence risk that deserves direct attention, while older, long-term users may need more support around physical health to stay engaged.
